big_idea: A repeating pattern is something that repeats in the same order — and we can use it to predict what comes next.
learning_intention: We are learning to identify and describe repeating patterns and to predict what comes next.
student_learning_goal: I can describe a repeating pattern and predict what comes next.
success_criteria: I can show or say what part of a pattern repeats.
I can predict what comes next in the parade and tell my partner what I see.
I can build my own repeating pattern with at least three different elements.
lesson_specific_materials: Printable Coco the Conductor puppet on a popsicle stick (1 for teacher; template included with manipulatives stage)
Class anchor chart paper labelled 'Pattern Parade — What we know'
Class diagnostic checklist (provided in assessment_suite stage)
Small drum or shaker for the clap-stomp warm-up
PATTERN word card (M6) ready to tape onto the anchor chart at the moment of introduction

minds_on.hook: Coco the Conductor is back, and this year he has a parade with more animals, more sounds, and a brand-new question for us: how do you KNOW what comes next?
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet in a circle. Hold up the Coco puppet. Say to students: 'Friends, last year (or in Kindergarten classrooms next door) Coco led parades and we just spotted what came next. This year, Coco wants more from us — he wants us to PREDICT what comes next AND tell him HOW WE KNOW. That is the Grade 1 job.'

Clap-stomp-jump warm-up: 'Watch and listen.' Demonstrate clap-stomp-jump, clap-stomp-jump, clap-stomp-jump. Pause. 'Eyes on me — what do you think comes next?' Take 3–4 predictions. Most will say 'clap'. Validate. 'How did you know it would be clap?' Listen. The first child who says 'because it goes clap-stomp-jump and then it starts again' has just described a repeating pattern.

Repeat the sequence once more, then say: 'When something keeps coming back the same way, in the same order, again and again, we call that a PATTERN. Say it with me — pattern.' Tape the PATTERN word card from M6 to the anchor chart. 'And when we say what comes next, we PREDICT.' Mime a small crystal-ball gesture. 'A pattern lets us predict because the order keeps coming back. Today we are going to PREDICT lots of parades.'
student_actions: Sit in a circle on the carpet.
Watch and copy the clap-stomp-jump sequence; predict what comes next when the teacher pauses.
Repeat the words 'pattern' and 'predict' aloud as a class.
Volunteer to explain HOW they knew what came next.

steps.instruction: Whole group: lay one Parade Strip (M2) flat in front of the carpet. Place Bea, Finn, Bea, Finn on the first four cells. Leave the fifth cell empty. Ask the class to read the parade aloud with you, then predict cell 5.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Coco's first parade today goes Bea, Finn, Bea, Finn… who do you predict comes next?' Take predictions. Place Bea on cell five. 'Yes — and how did you KNOW it was Bea? Tell your shoulder partner first.' (15 seconds.) 'Eyes back. What did you tell your partner?' Listen for: 'because Bea always comes after Finn' / 'because the parade keeps repeating Bea-Finn'. Validate the language of repetition.

steps.instruction: Show a second example with three animals: Bea, Finn, Bibi, Bea, Finn, Bibi, ?. Then a third with Bea, Bea, Finn, Bea, Bea, Finn, ?. Invite different children to place the next card and explain.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Coco's second parade is bigger. Bea, Finn, Bibi, Bea, Finn, Bibi… who comes next? Tell me, AND tell me why.' (Place card.) 'Now this one is sneaky. Bea, Bea, Finn, Bea, Bea, Finn… who comes next?' (Pause.) 'This one has TWO Beas before each Finn — does that count as a pattern?' Validate that yes, a pattern can have a repeated element. Hint that we will name these in tomorrow's lesson.

steps.instruction: Send children to partner spots. Each pair gets one set of Animal Cards (M1) and one Parade Strip (M2). Their job: build a parade pattern using two OR three different animals, repeat the rule across the strip, and leave the LAST cell empty for their partner to predict and explain.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'You and your partner are parade builders. Pick two or three animals — your choice. Build a parade where the pattern repeats. Leave the LAST cell empty. Then tap your partner and say: "What comes next, and how do you know?" Your partner has to PREDICT and EXPLAIN. Then swap.'

steps.instruction: Circulate. Use the diagnostic checklist to observe which children can extend a pattern, which can describe what repeats in their own words, which can justify a prediction (the new Grade 1 marker), and which can build a pattern with three different elements.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Ask one child: 'Can you read your partner's parade to me?' Then: 'What is the part that keeps repeating?' Then the Grade 1 question: 'And how do you KNOW what comes next?' Note responses on the diagnostic checklist.

differentiation.for_emerging: Pre-fill the first three cells of the parade strip with a simple AB pattern (Bea-Finn-Bea) and ask the child only to predict cells four and five. Pair with a confident partner. Allow oral prediction without needing to place the card.
differentiation.for_extending: Challenge the pair to build a 4-cell core with three different animals (e.g., Bea-Finn-Bibi-Finn). Then ask: 'If your parade had 10 cells, who would be in cell 10? How do you know?' This is foreshadowing tomorrow's rule lesson.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Use the animal name + a vest descriptor together when speaking ('Bea, the bear with the dark vest'). Allow the child to point or place a card instead of speaking. Accept gestures, sounds, or one-word responses as valid justifications. Photo cards of the animals available at the table.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: After building on the strip, the pair stands up and walks the parade — one child calls out animals, the other steps in time. The rhythm helps them feel the pattern.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Can the child predict the next element? Can they describe what is repeating, in their own words? Can they JUSTIFY their prediction even partially ('because the bear comes back')? Can they build their own repeating pattern with two or three elements without prompting?
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the appropriate column on the diagnostic checklist for each child as you circulate.

discussion_prompts: Who would like to share a parade you and your partner built? Read it out for us.
What was the part of your parade that kept coming back?
How did your partner KNOW what came next? What words did they use?
Did anyone find a pattern somewhere else in our classroom right now? (Floor tiles, calendar, clothing stripes, the alphabet strip on the wall — all count.)
consolidation.exit_routine: As children leave the carpet, each child names one place they will look for a pattern at home tonight AND says how they would predict the next part.

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Class diagnostic checklist completed during the partner-build phase. Captures baseline understanding of C1.1 — including the new Grade 1 marker of justification — before Lesson 2 introduces 'pattern rule' formally.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: This is the unit's diagnostic moment. The data tells the teacher who already extends and justifies a 2- or 3-element repeating pattern unprompted, so they can group flexibly for Lesson 2 onward. Children who only extend without justifying are typical for early Grade 1; children who already justify are ready for ABB / AAB rules in Lesson 2.

expanded_walkthrough.title: Building Their Own Pattern — and justifying the prediction
expanded_walkthrough.rationale: G1 Step 3 introduces TWO new demands: children can now choose between AB, ABB, AAB, or ABC, and they must JUSTIFY their next-element prediction out loud — the new G1 marker. This walkthrough covers how to detect whether a child has internalized the rule (rule-based extension) versus pattern-matched the immediate neighbour.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Each pair has a Parade Strip (M2), a full set of Animal Cards (M1), and a fresh sticky note. Teacher carries the diagnostic clipboard with a column for 'justifies aloud.' Carpet retains the three teacher-built examples (AB, ABC, AABA) for back-reference.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Walk to a pair that has built Bea-Bea-Finn-Bea-Bea-Finn-?. Don't ask 'what comes next?' — that lets them pattern-match the neighbour. Ask the harder question: 'What rule is your parade? Tell me out loud.' If the child says 'AAB,' confirm and ask the next move: 'So the eighth animal — what would it be? Tell me, and tell me HOW you know.' Wait for the verbal justification. The strong G1 answer references the rule: 'It's AAB, so after Bea-Bea-Finn comes Bea again because the rule starts over.' A weaker answer points at neighbours: 'Because Finn was just there so now it's Bea.'

Move to a pair attempting an ABC pattern (Bea-Finn-Bibi-Bea-Finn-Bibi-?). Ask: 'What comes next, and how would you explain it to a kindergartener?' Forcing them to translate the rule for a younger learner is the cleanest test of whether they own the rule. Listen for 'three friends, then they come back in the same order' — that's a strong G1 articulation.

Find a pair whose parade is technically correct but whose rule is fragile. Probe: 'If I picked TWO different animals — say, Moss and Bibi — could you build the SAME rule with them?' Watch whether the child can transfer the rule to new animals. Inability to transfer is your formative gate for L1: rule-naming is rote, not generative.

Record on the clipboard: who can name the rule, who can JUSTIFY a prediction with the rule, who can transfer the rule to new animals. Those three checkmarks scaffold the L2 cycle later in the week.
expected_student_responses: (Strong) 'It's AAB. So next is Bea-Bea-Finn-Bea-Bea-Finn-Bea, because after each Bea-Bea-Finn the rule starts over.'
(Mid) Names the rule but justifies by neighbours: 'Bea, because Finn was just there.'
(Confused) Names a rule that doesn't match what they built ('it's AB' but actually built ABB).
(Stretched) Builds with two animals, then voluntarily rebuilds the SAME rule using two different animals — articulates 'same rule, different friends.'
common_misconceptions: Naming the rule and applying it are the same skill. (Child can say 'AAB' but can't extend a strip — uses neighbour-matching instead.)
The rule is tied to specific animals. (Child can do AAB with Bea-Bea-Finn but not Moss-Moss-Bibi — hasn't generalized.)
Justification is repeating what you did. (Child says 'because I put Bea there' rather than 'because the rule says Bea comes next.')
recovery_moves: Force transfer to new animals. Hand the child a different pair (Moss + Bibi) and say 'same rule, different friends — go.' Inability to transfer is the diagnostic; the act of trying is often the unlock.
Insist on the WHY. When a child predicts the next element, follow with 'because…?' Wait. Most children can name the rule when forced. Some can't yet — that's L1 evidence.
Use the kindergarten-translator move. 'Pretend a four-year-old is here. How would you teach them this rule?' The translation pressure exposes whether the rule is internalized.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of C1.1 — describing a repeating pattern, predicting the next element, and creating an original repeating pattern.

parts_outline.task: Show a parade strip with Bea, Finn, Bea, Finn, ?. Student colours, draws, or stickers in the next animal AND traces / circles the words 'I predict ____ comes next because ____.'
Show a longer parade strip (8 cells) with the pattern Bea, Finn, Bibi, Bea, Finn, Bibi, Bea, ?. Student fills the last two cells based on the repeating rule.
Empty parade strip (6 cells) with a small key showing all four animals. Student creates their own repeating pattern using two OR three of the four parade animals (drawing or stickers).

expected_image_assets: Bea, Finn, Bibi, Moss thumbnail icons (for student to draw or for printed stickers)
Parade strip layout matching the M2 manipulative (5-cell, 8-cell, and 6-cell versions)
Coco the Conductor in the worksheet header
